NON-TRAUMATIC BACK PAIN 
 
 
 
RED FLAGS  
 
•
New pain at extremes of age (< 20 or >50) 
•
History of malignancy 
•
Constant, non-mechanical pain, or worse lying down/at night 
•
ANY neurology – weakness, numbness, paraesthesias etc. 
•
Bilateral symptoms 
•
Immune suppression (HIV, DM, steroids, immune suppressants) 
•
IV drug use 
•
Bowel/bladder function change, erectile dysfunction 
•
Fever, night sweats, weight loss 
•
Anticoagulant use e.g. warfarin 
GENERAL APPROACH 
One of the most common complaints in ED 
NB! History and examination more useful than special investigations. 
 
•
Majority of NON-TRAUMA cases are benign musculoskeletal lower back pain 
•
Physical exam concerning features: 
§
Motor: arm/leg weakness, especially bilateral 
§
Sensory: saddle anaesthesia, paraesthesia, sensory level 
§
Reflexes: any abnormal reflexes, including babinski 
§
Sphincter dysfunction: decreased rectal tone, urinary retention/incontinence 
§
Midline spinal tenderness, deformity, swelling, fluctuance 
§
Systemic: wasting, fever, lymphadenopathy, other pathologic fractures 
•
Imaging: Spinal x-rays are neither sensitive nor specific 
•
Back pain with new neurology, or suspicion for epidural abscess requires urgent MRI 
•
Lab workup for underlying condition as indicated 
SPINE RELATED CAUSES 
 
•
Infectious: Spinal epidural abscess, vertebral osteomyelitis, infectious discitis, TB spine 
•
Oncological: Pathological fracture, bone or epidural metastases, spinal tumours 
•
Haematological: Spinal epidural haematoma – anticoagulants, recent lumbar 
puncture/epidural anaesthesia/spinal surgery 
•
Neurological: Cauda equina syndrome, disc herniation causing cord compression 
•
Degenerative: Spondylolysis/spondylolisthesis/OA with radiculopathy 
 
SPECIFIC MANAGEMENT 
•
Epidural abscess: Antibiotics – Consider Ceftriaxone, Cefazolin or Vancomycin 
•
Suspected metastases: Dexamethasone 10mg IV stat, urgent MRI 
 
DISPOSITION 
 
•
Low risk patients: Non-specific pain < 6 weeks with no 
red flags, monoradiculopathy/sciatica – DC with simple 
analgesics and physio/spine OPD follow up 
•
High risk patients – manage underlying cause, admit to 
appropriate subspecialty once stable 
Dr du Plessis / Dr R Gihwala CMJAH Emergency Department June 2020 
NON-SPINE RELATED CAUSES 
•
VASCULAR: AAA, aortic dissection, renal artery 
dissection/thrombosis 
•
RENAL: renal colic, pyelonephritis, perinephric abscess, prostatitis 
•
GIT: pancreatitis, PUD, cholecystitis 
•
ANTICOAGULANTS: retroperitoneal haemorrhage 
•
GYNAE: PID, rarely ectopic pregnancy. Lower back pain is common 
in PREGNANCY
